feedback.message: Not yet — `c` is `const`. Can a move constructor, which must modify its source, take a `const` object?

hints: `std::move` only casts. Which constructor can accept a `const std::vector<int>&&`?
A vector's move constructor leaves the source empty.
exercises.solution: It prints `0 3 2 2`. `w` is move-constructed from `v`, which a vector's move constructor leaves empty. But `c` is `const`: `std::move(c)` produces a `const std::vector<int>&&`, which cannot bind to the move constructor's `std::vector<int>&&` parameter, so the **copy** constructor is chosen and `c` keeps its two elements. No warning, no error, just a silent copy. This is why objects you intend to move from should not be `const`.

feedback.message: Not yet — what does `q.reset()` do to the count?
Not yet — `r` was assigned from `s` inside the block and outlives it.

hints: Count the `shared_ptr` objects that currently point at the int, line by line.
`s` dies at the end of the block; `reset()` makes `q` empty.
exercises.solution: Owners after each step: `p` (1), `q` (2), `s` (3), `r = s` (4), end of block destroys `s` (3), `q.reset()` (2). The remaining owners are `p` and `r`, so it prints **2**.

feedback.message: Not yet — in the second block `c` and `d` own each other. When the locals go away, does either count reach zero?
Not yet — `b` is still owned by `a->next` after the local `b` is destroyed, so it cannot die before `a`.

hints: In the first block, the local `b` is destroyed first, but is it the last owner of node b?
In the second block, draw the owners of each node after both locals are gone.
exercises.solution: It prints `ab||`. In the first block, local `b` is destroyed first, but node b is still owned by `a->next`. Then local `a` goes, node a's count reaches 0, its destructor prints `a`, and destroying its `next` member releases node b, which prints `b`. In the second block, c and d own each other: when the locals are destroyed each count drops to 1, never 0, so neither destructor runs. That is a leak. Making one of the links a `std::weak_ptr` fixes it.

options.label: It casts `x` to an rvalue reference, so that overload resolution can choose a move constructor or move assignment.
options.feedback: Yes. All the actual moving is done by whichever constructor or assignment operator is then chosen.

options.label: It moves `x`'s contents to a new location in memory.
options.feedback: Not yet — `std::move(x);` on a line by itself does nothing at all. It only changes how the expression is treated.

options.label: It destroys `x`.
options.feedback: Not yet — `x` is still alive and will be destroyed normally at the end of its scope.

options.label: It makes `x` empty.
options.feedback: Not yet — any emptying is done by the move constructor or assignment that receives the cast, if one does.

hints: Consider the statement `std::move(x);` with nothing receiving the result.
exercises.solution: `std::move` is a cast to an rvalue reference (`static_cast<T&&>(x)`, roughly). It signals that you will not use `x`'s value again, which allows a move constructor or move assignment to be selected. If nothing receives the result, or the receiver has no move overload, nothing is moved.

exercises.prompt: A class has a move constructor that is correct but **not** marked `noexcept`. What changes when objects of this class are stored in a `std::vector` that grows?

options.label: When the vector reallocates, it copies the existing elements instead of moving them, if the class can be copied.
options.feedback: Yes. To keep its guarantee that a failed reallocation leaves the vector unchanged, the vector only moves elements whose move cannot throw.

options.label: The program fails to compile.
options.feedback: Not yet — it compiles. The difference is in which constructor the vector chooses.

options.label: Nothing: `noexcept` is documentation only.
options.feedback: Not yet — the library inspects `noexcept` at compile time (with `std::move_if_noexcept`) and changes its behaviour.

options.label: The program terminates whenever the vector grows.
options.feedback: Not yet — termination happens if a `noexcept` function *does* throw. Here the function is not marked at all.

hints: What does `std::vector` promise if an exception occurs while it is moving elements to new memory?
exercises.solution: `std::vector` gives the *strong exception guarantee* when it reallocates: if anything throws, the vector is as it was. If a move might throw halfway through, some elements would already have been moved out of the old buffer and the guarantee would be broken. So the vector moves only when the move constructor is `noexcept` (or the type cannot be copied at all), and otherwise copies. A missing `noexcept` can turn every reallocation into a full copy, which is why the rule is: move operations should be `noexcept`.

exercises.prompt: Which of these choices match the ownership guidelines in this lesson? Select all that apply.

options.label: A function that prints a shape's area takes `const Shape&`.
options.feedback: Yes. It only uses the shape, so it should not involve ownership at all.

options.label: A `Scene` that owns many shapes of different derived types stores a `std::vector` of `std::unique_ptr` to `Shape`.
options.feedback: Yes. Each shape has one owner, and the vector of unique pointers lets different types live behind one interface.

options.label: Every function that receives a shape takes a `std::shared_ptr` to `Shape` by value, just in case.
options.feedback: Not yet — passing a `shared_ptr` by value claims co-ownership and costs atomic reference-count updates. Functions that only use an object should take a reference.

options.label: A cache entry that should not keep an expensive object alive, but wants to use it if it still exists, holds a `std::weak_ptr`.
options.feedback: Yes. That is exactly the "observe without owning, and check it is still there" relationship.

options.label: A class creates its helper with `new Helper` and stores the raw pointer, deleting it in the destructor.
options.feedback: Not yet — that is the rule of five done by hand, and easy to get wrong. A `std::unique_ptr` member, created with `std::make_unique`, does it all.

hints: For each case, ask: who owns the object, and does this piece of code need to own it?
exercises.solution: (a), (b) and (d) match. Code that only *uses* an object takes a reference; sole ownership is a value or a `unique_ptr`; observing a `shared_ptr`-owned object that may vanish is a `weak_ptr`. (c) spreads ownership where none is needed, and (e) manages memory by hand where `std::unique_ptr` would do it automatically.
